title: Area IX review: Emergency Operations
intro: These questions mix the two Tasks of Area IX in this course: loss of communications, and an approach with loss of primary flight instrument indicators. (The multiengine Tasks C and D are not part of this course.) Most put both in one flight the way your learner may meet them: an alternator failure that takes the radios and then the PFD, a radio failure in a hold while flying partial panel, a no-gyro radar approach that loses its controller, a static blockage on a no-radio approach, and the safe ways to practice it all in the airplane and the training device.

questions.q: Your instrument learner is in IMC at 6,000 feet in a round-dial Cessna 172, 70 minutes from his destination. The alternator light comes on, the ammeter shows a discharge, and the POH reset does not work. The radios still work, and a towered airport with an ILS is 12 miles away. What do you have him do now?
options: Squawk 7600 to warn ATC early, shed load, and plan to fly 91.185 to his destination if the radios then quit
Tell ATC about the coming electrical failure, shed load, and get a clearance to the nearby airport while he can talk
Turn the master off to save the battery, then fly the filed route with no radio and begin the approach right at his ETA
Keep the clearance to his destination, but ask for a lower altitude so he can look for VFR conditions under the clouds
questions.why: If the alternator cannot be reset, advise ATC of the situation and of the impending electrical failure [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. No pilot should consider continuing once the charging system has failed: reduce the electrical load and land at the nearest suitable airport, and the IFH's figure of about 40 minutes of battery is an approximation not to be relied on [[23:330|IFH 11-5]]. The AFH adds: notify ATC immediately and request radar vectors to the nearest suitable airport [[24:363|AFH 18-14]]. Asking now also fixes the lost comm plan: if the radios die later, he flies the route assigned in the last ATC clearance received [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(c)(1)]], which now leads to the nearby airport. Code 7600 is for a loss of two-way radio capability that has already happened [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]], and 70 minutes of 91.185 on a dying battery is not a plan.

questions.q: In IMC the alternator fails in your learner's glass-panel airplane, which is wired like the IFH example. With the standby battery armed, he switches the MASTER battery side off, as the IFH describes. Approach control, which he had on COM2, goes silent at once. He says, "Radios failed, squawking 7600." What do you teach?
options: He is right: a radio that goes quiet just after a change in power is a real failure, so he squawks 7600 and flies 91.185
Turn the battery master back on, because every radio needs main battery power until he is ready to fly the approach
Call on 121.5 using COM2, since the emergency frequency still works on a radio that has lost its normal source of power
Check before calling it lost comm: select COM1 and set Approach there, as the essential bus usually feeds Com 1
questions.why: With the MASTER side off, the standby battery comes online to power the essential bus, which usually powers the AHRS, ADC, PFD, Nav 1, Com 1 and the standby indicator light [[23:331|IFH 11-6]]; Com 2 is not on that list. Switching the transmitter selector between COM1 and COM2 changes both the transmit and receive frequencies [[23:54|IFH 2-3]]. Recognizing a radio failure starts with checking volume and frequency [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2]], and 7600 is for a real loss of two-way radio capability [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]]. The technique saves the main battery for the approach, when flaps, gear and lights may need it [[23:331|IFH 11-6]], so turning it back on throws that away, and a radio with no power cannot reach 121.5 either.

questions.q: Thirty minutes after an alternator failure left his round-dial airplane with no radios at all, your learner, still in IMC, comes out of the clouds into VFR conditions. A towered airport is 10 miles ahead; his destination is 40 minutes away. What do you teach?
options: Stay VFR and land at the towered field: wait outside its surface area to see the traffic flow, join the pattern, look for a steady green
Stay VFR but go on to his destination, since "as soon as practicable" means he never has to land short of the airport he filed to
Climb back into the clouds and keep flying 91.185, since the flight began under IFR and ATC is still protecting his route for him
Fly straight in to the runway in use and land when the tower shows a flashing green, its light signal that he is cleared to land
questions.why: If VFR conditions are encountered after the failure, the pilot shall continue the flight under VFR and land as soon as practicable [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(b)]]. The AIM note says that is not "as soon as possible": the pilot need not land at an unauthorized or unsuitable airport, or only minutes short of the destination [[34:53|AIM 6-4-1]]. Forty minutes is not minutes short, and with a failed charging system the IFH says to land at the nearest suitable airport [[23:330|IFH 11-5]]. With the transmitter and receiver both out, remain outside or above the Class D surface area until the direction and flow of traffic is known, then join the pattern and keep visual contact with the tower for light signals [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13]]. In flight a steady green means cleared to land, while a flashing green means return for landing [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].

questions.q: Your learner reported a vacuum failure and is flying partial panel when Center gives him the PINNE holding clearance shown in the figure. PINNE is not a fix from which an approach begins, and his ETA from the filed ETE is 1710. At 1620, while holding, the radios fail. What does he do?
options: Leave PINNE at once, since a radio failure cancels the hold, and start the approach as soon as he reaches the approach fix
Hold at PINNE until 1710, his ETA, then fly to a fix where an approach begins and start the approach on arrival there
Keep holding with timed standard-rate turns, then leave PINNE at 1645 and begin the approach as close as possible to 1710
Leave PINNE at 1645 and begin the approach on reaching the approach fix, since the EFC now sets the time to start it
questions.why: When the clearance limit is not a fix from which an approach begins, the pilot leaves it at the EFC time if one was received, proceeds to a fix from which an approach begins, and commences descent or descent and approach as close as possible to the ETA calculated from the filed or amended ETE [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(3)(ii)]]. The EFC is in the clearance so that, with lost comm, the pilot can leave the holding fix at a definite time [[29:111|IPH 2-51]]; here it sets the leaving time, not the approach time, and the ETA does not set the leaving time. Holding turns are made at 3 degrees per second or 30 degrees of bank, whichever needs less bank [[33:391|AIM 5-3-8]]. With no heading indicator that means timed turns on the calibrated turn coordinator, rolling out when the computed seconds have passed [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

questions.q: After a vacuum failure en route in IMC, which he has reported, your learner slows from his filed 120 knots true airspeed to 100 to make partial panel easier. The flight will now take about 15 minutes longer than his filed ETE. The radios still work. What should he tell ATC, and why does it matter if the radios fail later?
options: Nothing: ATC sees his groundspeed on radar, and 91.185 sets his ETA from the time at which his radios failed
Nothing yet: if the radios fail, he may add the 15 minutes to his filed ETE himself, as 91.185 allows him to
Ask for an EFC at his destination, since after an instrument failure 91.185 uses the EFC in place of an ETA
Report the change in true airspeed and give ATC a new estimate, so that his ETE is amended with ATC
questions.why: Pilots report, at all times, a change in average true airspeed at cruise of 5 percent or 10 knots, whichever is greater, from the airspeed filed [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]]; 20 knots is more than both. That matters for lost comm because 91.185 times the approach from the ETA "calculated from the filed or amended (with ATC) estimated time en route" [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(3)]]. An ETE he changes on his own is not amended with ATC, so ATC would still expect the filed time, and the rule never uses the time the radios failed. An EFC is used when one has been received [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(3)(i)]], not because an instrument failed.

questions.q: Your learner's heading indicator has failed, and he is flying a no-gyro surveillance approach. Before it began the controller said, "If no transmission received for one minute, climb to 3,000, proceed direct to the VOR and fly the VOR Runway 9 approach." On final the controller goes silent for over a minute, and calls on the last frequency bring no answer. What does he do?
options: Hold the last heading and keep descending to the MDA, since guidance on final needs no reply from him
Fly the instructions given before the approach, which ATC issued in place of the general lost comm rule
Fly 91.185 to his filed destination, since only the regulation, not a controller, can set a lost comm route
Climb to the MEA and hold at the VOR until his ETA, then fly the VOR approach from its initial approach fix
questions.why: "If no transmission received for (time)" is the phrase ATC uses in radar approaches to prefix the procedures the pilot should follow in the event of lost communications [[34:361|P/CG I-2]], and radar controllers issue them when IFR weather is likely during the approach [[34:374|P/CG L-3]]. 91.185 applies "unless otherwise authorized by ATC" [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(a)]], so the controller's instructions come first, and neither 91.185 to the filed destination nor holding to the ETA is what ATC now expects. Pressing on to the MDA ignores that a radar approach needs a functioning transmitter and receiver, and that on a surveillance approach the controller gives the only guidance, in azimuth only [[33:430|AIM 5-4-11]]. The no-gyro pilot turns only on the controller's "turn right," "stop turn" [[33:431|AIM 5-4-11]], so with silence he has nothing to steer by.

questions.q: Your learner, partial panel after an AHRS failure, is cleared direct to the VOR that is both his clearance limit and the initial approach fix: "Maintain 6,000, expect 4,000 in ten minutes." The MEA is 4,000, and no EFC was given. Four minutes later the radios fail; his ETA is 25 minutes away. Eager to get out of the clouds, he wants to start down. What altitude does he fly?
options: 6,000, the higher of assigned and minimum, until he begins descent and approach as close as possible to his computed ETA
4,000 once the ten minutes are up, because an expected altitude replaces the assigned one at its specified time
4,000 right away, since on partial panel the minimum IFR altitude becomes the altitude the rule wants him to fly
6,000 to the VOR, then 4,000 in the hold there, so he is already lower and ready to start the approach when the ETA comes
questions.why: When the expect clearance gives a lower altitude, the pilot keeps the higher of the last assigned altitude and the minimum IFR altitude until the time or fix in the leave clearance limit rule [[34:54|AIM 6-4-1]]. The rule itself takes the highest of assigned, minimum and expected for the segment being flown [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(2)]], and at a clearance limit that is a fix from which an approach begins, with no EFC, he commences descent or descent and approach as close as possible to the ETA [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(3)(i)]]. Only a higher expected altitude is flown from its time or fix [[34:54|AIM 6-4-1]], so the ten-minute mark changes nothing, and nothing in the rule lets the minimum altitude replace a higher assigned one or allows a descent in the hold before the ETA.

questions.q: On a real IFR flight plan in VMC, with you in the right seat, you want your learner to practice a partial panel approach and his lost comm plan on the same flight. Which setup is both legal and realistic?
options: Turn the radio volume down and have him fly the 91.185 route and timing for real, since ATC protects a no-radio airplane
Have him squawk 7600 for a few minutes so the controller sees RDOF, then go back to his code and fly the approach
Keep the watch on the real frequency, cover his gyros with you as safety pilot, and have him say his lost comm plan out loud
Cover his gyros and work the charts with him heads-down, since an IFR flight plan removes the need for a safety pilot
questions.why: Under IFR in controlled airspace the pilot in command must ensure a continuous watch on the appropriate frequency [[60:482|14 CFR 91.183]], so the lost comm part is talked through, not flown. Code 7600 makes the data block flash RDOF to alert the controller [[29:107|IPH 2-47]], and ATC then serves the flight on the basis that the pilot is flying 91.185 [[34:53|AIM 6-4-1]], so neither a practice squawk nor a silent radio belongs in training. Simulated instrument flight needs a safety pilot in the other control seat with at least a private pilot certificate for the category and class [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]], adequate vision forward and to each side [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]], and fully functioning dual controls [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(3)]]; an IFR flight plan changes none of that.

questions.q: In IMC on vectors, your learner's PFD suddenly looks like the figure. The radios still work. What do you teach him to do?
options: Fly the standby instruments, engage the wing leveler as the maker recommends, then report and ask for no-gyro vectors
Steer by the heading bug on the HSI, still set to 273°, and report the failure once he is established on the final course
Wait for reversionary mode to bring attitude and air data back on the MFD, then tell ATC what happened
Squawk 7700 and stop talking to ATC, since losing the PFD leaves him no spare attention at all for the radio work
questions.why: This is the IFH's AHRS and ADC failure: with no attitude shown, the only references left are the standby airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and magnetic compass, and the manufacturer recommends turning on the autopilot, a wing leveler, to cut workload and the chance of an unusual attitude [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. An AHRS failure removes all heading and attitude indications from the PFD [[23:217|IFH 7-56]], so the 273° in the box is only the bug setting, not his heading. Reversionary mode is what the system does when a display fails [[23:329|IFH 11-4]], and this is a sensor failure. The usual next step is to advise ATC and, if necessary, declare an emergency [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]; a pilot whose stabilized compass is inoperative asks for a no-gyro vector or approach [[33:431|AIM 5-4-11]], and in radio contact he keeps his assigned code [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

questions.q: On your checkride the examiner plays your learner. On vectors in IMC he has a vacuum failure, covers the gyros, squawks 7600 and says, "I'll go no-radio so I can concentrate on flying." The radios work fine. How do you analyze and correct it?
options: Accept it: 7600 tells ATC he is too busy to talk, and ATC must then protect his route and altitude under 91.185
Fix only the code: he should squawk 7700 and then stay off the radio until the airplane is safely on the ground
Name it failure to notify ATC: keep his code, report the failure, and ask for help such as no-gyro vectors
Accept it, as long as he also flies the 91.185 route and timing, since he has chosen to stop talking to ATC
questions.why: Failure to notify ATC of the situation is one of the PTS common errors for this Task (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area IX, Task B). Code 7600 is for a loss of two-way radio capability [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]], and a pilot in radio contact keeps squawking his assigned code [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]. Code 7700 alerts a ground radar facility, after which the pilot should immediately establish communications [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2]], not go silent. A pilot doubtful about any condition that could affect flight safety is already in at least an urgency condition, and that is the time to ask for help [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. The report gives the equipment affected, the impairment and the help wanted [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]], and with a dead heading indicator that help is a no-gyro vector or approach [[33:431|AIM 5-4-11]].

questions.q: Partial panel after a vacuum failure in IMC, your learner plans to ask for a no-gyro surveillance approach at his destination. His clearance limit is the IAF of the destination's VOR approach, with no EFC. Thirty minutes out, the radios fail completely. What changes in his plan?
options: Nothing: once ATC sees RDOF it will still run the no-gyro approach, and he follows the turn calls as before
He must hold at the IAF until he finds VFR conditions, since no approach may be flown without the gyros
He begins the VOR approach the moment he reaches the IAF, since the ETA rule applies only to full panels
No radar approach without a working radio: he flies the VOR approach himself on partial panel, starting near his ETA
questions.why: The only airborne radio equipment a radar approach needs is a functioning transmitter and receiver [[33:430|AIM 5-4-11]], and on a no-gyro approach the pilot turns only when he hears "turn right" or "stop turn" [[33:431|AIM 5-4-11]], so with both gone there is no radar approach. At a clearance limit that is a fix from which an approach begins, with no EFC, he commences descent or descent and approach as close as possible to the ETA [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(3)(i)]]; nothing in the rule changes that for partial panel. No source forbids an approach without the gyros: the PTS requires a nonprecision approach without them (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area VIII NOTE), and the IFH says to practice flying without the attitude and heading indicators for just this failure [[23:333|IFH 11-8]].

questions.q: His radios dead in IMC, your learner begins the VOR approach at his ETA as 91.185 requires. Descending after the FAF, his altimeter unwinds slowly, the VSI shows far less than his planned rate, and the airspeed reads higher than it should. What is happening, and what does he do?
options: A pitot blockage: he ignores the airspeed and keeps the descent going on the altimeter, which is unaffected
A partial static blockage: he opens the alternate static source and keeps it if the needles move a lot
A vacuum failure: he covers the attitude and heading indicators and flies the rest of the approach partial panel
Normal lag in a descent: he pushes the nose over until the altimeter and VSI catch up with his plan
questions.why: A partial static blockage may go unrecognized until the airplane begins a descent [[24:363|AFH 18-14]]; then the instruments show it too high, too fast and descending much more slowly than desired [[24:364|AFH 18-15]]. The fix is to open the alternate static source while climbing or descending: if the needles move significantly, a static problem exists and the alternate source is used for the rest of the flight [[24:364|AFH 18-15]]. Expect the altimeter and airspeed to read slightly high, with a brief climb on the VSI [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]. A pitot blockage leaves altitude and vertical speed unaffected [[24:364|AFH 18-15]], so it cannot explain the altimeter and VSI here, and pushing over to chase the needles would put him lower than he thinks he is.

questions.q: Your learner flies a round-dial PA-28 with a vacuum attitude indicator and heading indicator and an electric turn coordinator. In IMC the alternator fails, and later the battery dies, taking the radios with it. Which flight instruments does he still have?
options: Only the compass and the pitot-static instruments, because the gyro instruments also need electrical power
All six, because in a round-dial airplane every flight instrument runs on vacuum or pitot-static pressure
Attitude and heading indicators, airspeed, altimeter, VSI and compass; the turn coordinator dies with the radios
The turn coordinator and the pitot-static instruments, since the vacuum pump needs the alternator to keep running
questions.why: The vacuum pump is driven mechanically off the engine [[23:332|IFH 11-7]], and many airplanes with pneumatic attitude indicators use electric rate indicators [[23:112|IFH 5-17]], so here the electric turn coordinator fails with the battery while the vacuum gyros keep working. The magnetic compass is independent of other instruments and power sources [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. Round-dial airplanes rely less on electrical power for the primary instruments than glass ones [[23:331|IFH 11-6]], but that does not mean all six survive. Pilots should know which systems are electric and which keep working without power [[23:331|IFH 11-6]] [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. Application: a learner who has only practiced with the attitude and heading indicators covered may not expect to lose the turn coordinator instead.

questions.q: Debriefing an alternator failure in the training device, your glass-panel learner asks what he would have had if he had flown 91.185 all the way to his ETA and both the main and the standby battery had run out in IMC. What do you answer?
options: Standby instruments only, and pilotage and dead reckoning unless he carries a handheld GPS transceiver
Com 1 and Nav 1 on the essential bus, which the engine itself keeps powered once both batteries are empty
The PFD in reversionary mode on the MFD, which keeps its own reserve of power for the approach and landing
The standby instruments and the MFD moving map, which has an internal battery for failures just like this
questions.why: Do not rely on any power after the standby battery has exhausted itself; the flight deck may become very dark [[23:331|IFH 11-6]]. The standby attitude indicator, altimeter, airspeed indicator and magnetic compass would be the only instruments left, and navigation would be limited to pilotage and dead reckoning unless a hand-held transceiver with a GPS or navigation function is on board [[23:331|IFH 11-6]]. The essential bus, with Com 1, Nav 1 and the PFD, is what the standby battery powers [[23:331|IFH 11-6]], so it goes dark with it. That is why the IFH treats the failure as an emergency in technically advanced aircraft and says to reduce the load and land as soon as practical [[23:331|IFH 11-6]], not stretch the battery to an ETA.

questions.q: Cruising level in cloud at a steady power setting in a glass-panel airplane, with no ice on the wings, your learner sees the PFD airspeed slowly fall toward zero, and the standby airspeed indicator does the same. Altitude and vertical speed stay steady. He reaches for full power and lowers the nose. What do you teach?
options: Good reaction: two airspeed indicators agree, so the airplane really is slowing toward a stall and needs power
A static blockage: open the alternate static source, which also gives the standby indicator its own pressure
An AHRS failure: fly the standby attitude indicator and ask ATC for no-gyro vectors to the nearest airport
Likely a pitot blockage feeding both: pitot heat on, hold pitch and power, trust the altimeter and VSI, and report
questions.why: If the pitot opening is blocked but the drain hole is open, the indicated airspeed slowly drops to zero [[23:97|IFH 5-2]] [[23:98|IFH 5-3]], while a pitot blockage leaves altitude and vertical speed unaffected [[24:364|AFH 18-15]]. Many light airplanes with glass displays feed the backup instruments from the same pitot-static inputs, so both can fail together [[24:364|AFH 18-15]]: two indicators agreeing proves nothing here. The AFH lists failing to engage pitot heat in IMC among the ways pilots end up in unpracticed partial panel flight [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. A static blockage makes the airspeed read wrong only as the airplane climbs or descends away from the altitude where the ports blocked [[23:98|IFH 5-3]], so it does not explain an airspeed falling toward zero in level cruise. Other failed equipment that affects safety or IFR capability is reported to ATC [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]].

questions.q: In the training device you fail your learner's AHRS and his radios at the same moment. He fixates on the PFD keys, forgets the radio, and drifts 300 feet. How do you build the next lessons?
options: Give him the same double failure every session, since the combined failure is what he must handle on the checkride
Practice each failure alone until he handles it reasonably well, then combine them, mixing the order at random
Move him to the airplane now, where real workload will cure the fixation faster than the device
Drill one failure at a time in the same fixed order each lesson, since that blocked practice gives the best retention
questions.why: Before learners perform several tasks at once, each task should be practiced until it can be done reasonably well in isolation, and fixation is often a sign that a task has not had enough practice alone [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. Random practice gives better retention than blocked practice, even though blocked practice scores better during the session itself [[25:78|AIH 3-27]], so a fixed order is the wrong drill. The FAA recommends that training continue in the simulator until the tasks are done successfully, before trying them in an aircraft [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].
